props.title: Gypo
props.initialSlug: A story of betrayal and guilt.

sections.content: Gypo marked a groundbreaking moment in British independent cinema as the first UK Dogme 95 certified film. Director Jan Dunn crafted this raw exploration of xenophobia and family breakdown in a working-class Kent community, using handheld cameras and natural lighting per Dogme rules. The film's power comes from Pauline McLynn's devastating performance as Helen, a woman whose life unravels after befriending a Czech refugee. Like Ken Loach's Sweet Sixteen (2002) and Red Road (2006), Gypo strips away cinematic artifice to expose harsh social realities.

sections.content: The film's exploration of immigration tensions echoes throughout contemporary British cinema, from Dirty Pretty Things (2002) to In This World (2002). But where those films take broader political perspectives, Gypo burrows into intimate domestic spaces. The handheld camerawork creates an almost documentary feel, similar to Andrea Arnold's Fish Tank (2009) or Shane Meadows' This Is England (2006), where social commentary emerges organically through character interaction rather than overt messaging.

As a Dogme 95 film, Gypo follows the movement's strict "Vow of Chastity" rules - no artificial lighting, only handheld cameras, no non-diegetic music. Like fellow Dogme films The Idiots (1998) and Mifune (1999), this technical austerity creates an immediacy that heightens emotional impact. The approach particularly serves the film's intimate family drama, where every facial expression and gesture carries heightened significance. SUBHEAD: British Social Realism and Immigration

sections.content: Gypo sits within a vital tradition of British films examining immigration and cultural identity, from Beautiful Thing (1996) to Last Resort (2000). Director Jan Dunn brings a feminist perspective to this lineage, focusing on how women's lives intersect with broader social issues. The film's portrayal of female friendship across cultural divides recalls Ae Fond Kiss (2004) while maintaining the kitchen-sink realism of films like Nil By Mouth (1997).
